1. Core Clinical Tension: A 28-year-old female presents with an 8-month history of an enlarging hypopigmented, hypoesthetic patch on the lower extremity accompanied by palpable common peroneal nerve thickening. The presence of intersecting linear tattoo markings applied by a village traditional healer reflects traditional cultural attempts to physically contain lesion margins, which delayed medical evaluation. The diagnostic challenge involves distinguishing tuberculoid mycobacterial nerve invasion from non-infectious hypopigmented disorders and granulomatous dermatoses in an afebrile young patient.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs at outpatient dermatologic physical examination demonstrating cutaneous hypoesthesia and palpable peripheral nerve enlargement, prior to slit-skin smear examination, high-resolution nerve ultrasonography, and punch skin biopsy histopathology.
3. Differential Distinctions: Vitiligo or post-inflammatory hypopigmentation (lack sensory loss or peripheral nerve thickening), tinea corporis / dermatophytosis (retains sensation and lacks nerve enlargement), cutaneous leishmaniasis / lupus vulgaris (lack localized anesthesia and nerve hypertrophy), and sarcoidosis (granulomatous but without neural enlargement). Slit-skin smears are frequently paucibacillary/negative in tuberculoid spectrum disease, making nerve thickening and biopsy showing epithelioid and Langhans' giant cell granulomas confirmatory.
case_prompt:
A 28-year-old female presented to the dermatology outpatient clinic with an 8-month history of an enlarging patch below her right knee. The lesion had begun as a small, pea-sized spot that progressively expanded in size, accompanied by noticeable loss of temperature and light touch sensations over the area. Due to cultural beliefs, the patient had consulted a village traditional practitioner who applied two sets of intersecting tattoo markings over the lesion in an attempt to demarcate and contain its spread, which delayed her presentation for conventional medical care.

On cutaneous examination, there was a well-defined, hypopigmented patch measuring 5 x 6 cm located below the right knee, extending to both the medial and lateral aspects of the leg. Neurological testing of the lesion demonstrated complete absence of thermal sensation and distinctly diminished light touch sensation. Palpation of peripheral nerve trunks revealed marked palpable thickening and enlargement of the right common peroneal nerve. Systemic physical examination and vital signs were otherwise unremarkable.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Although presenting as a discrete hypopigmented macule, vitiligo and post-inflammatory pigmentary alterations demonstrate fully preserved thermal, tactile, and pinprick sensations and are never associated with peripheral nerve enlargement.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On cutaneous examination, a hypopigmented patch of size 5x6 cm below knee extending to medial and lateral side of leg, which was associated with absent temperature sensation and decreased touch sensation. On nerve palpation thickening of the right common peroneal nerve was present.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Cutaneous tuberculosis (lupus vulgaris) or cutaneous sarcoidosis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: While both disorders may produce dermal epithelioid granulomas, neither causes localized thermal anesthesia with prominent regional peripheral nerve trunk hypertrophy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: High resolution ultrasonography of the right common peroneal nerve revealed enlarged cross-sectional area (Figure 3 (Fig. 3)).

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot was established by the triad of an anesthetic hypopigmented plaque, palpable common peroneal nerve thickening confirmed by high-resolution ultrasonography showing an increased cross-sectional area, and full-thickness punch skin biopsy revealing epithelioid cells and Langhans' giant cells, confirming borderline tuberculoid leprosy despite a negative slit-skin smear.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Slit skin smear for AFB leprae was negative. A skin biopsy was done from the lesion and revealed epithelioid cells with Langhans' giant cells (Figure 2 (Fig. 2)). High resolution ultrasonography of the right common peroneal nerve revealed enlarged cross-sectional area (Figure 3 (Fig. 3))... Patient was eventually diagnosed with borderline tuberculoid leprosy (Ridley-Jopling classification)

editor_comments: Distilled case accurately targets Leprosy (borderline tuberculoid leprosy). Breakpoint placed after cutaneous sensory and nerve examination, before slit-skin smear and biopsy. Zero pathogen disclosures.
